SECTION 010:00–4:20

One system, three pictures

The row picture, the column picture, and Ax = b.

The central problem of this lecture is to solve a system of linear equations. Strang begins with the square case: n equations in n unknowns. He then presents three ways to see the same problem.

01

Row picture

Read one equation at a time. Each equation describes a geometric set of possible solutions.

02

Column picture

Read one column at a time. Choose coefficients that combine the columns into the right-hand side.

03

Matrix form

Write all the equations together as Ax = b.

The first example is

2x − y = 0
−x + 2y = 3.

The coefficient matrix contains the numbers multiplying the unknowns. The unknowns form a vector, and the right-hand sides form another vector:

[2−1−12][xy]=[03]

Here A is the 2 × 2 matrix, the unknown vector is (x, y)T, and b is (0, 3)T. The next two sections explain what this compact equation means geometrically.

SECTION 024:20–8:39

The row picture: two lines meet

Read one equation at a time and look for the common point.

For the first equation, 2x − y = 0, each solution is a point in the xy-plane. Both (0, 0) and (1, 2) satisfy it. All its solutions lie on the line y = 2x.

The second equation, −x + 2y = 3, gives a different line. It passes through (−3, 0) and (−1, 1), the points Strang uses to draw it. It does not pass through the origin, because substituting x = y = 0 gives 0 rather than 3.

A solution of the system must satisfy both equations at once. In the row picture, it must lie on both lines. Their intersection is

x = 1,   y = 2.

Check it directly in the original rows:

2(1) − 2 = 0
−1 + 2(2) = 3.

The two lines tell the same story as the two equations: there is one common point, (1, 2).

SECTION 038:39–15:27

The column picture: build b from columns

A linear combination turns two columns into the desired vector.

Now group the x-terms together and the y-terms together. Instead of two separate row equations, read the system as one vector equation:

x[2−1]+y[−12]=[03]

Call the columns a₁ = (2, −1)T and a₂ = (−1, 2)T. The unknowns x and y are the amounts of those columns needed to make b. Multiplying vectors by numbers and adding them is a linear combination.

We already know the right coefficients: x = 1 and y = 2. Start at the origin and draw one copy of a₁. From its tip, add a₂, then add another a₂. The successive endpoints are

(0, 0) → (2, −1) → (1, 1) → (0, 3).

The endpoint is precisely b. Entry by entry, 2 + 2(−1) = 0 and −1 + 2(2) = 3.

What if we allow every x and every y?

Strang then asks about all combinations of these two columns. For this particular pair, the combinations fill the whole plane. Thus every two-component right-hand side can be reached by choosing suitable coefficients. This broader question will return in three dimensions.

SECTION 0415:27–21:59

Three equations become three planes

The row picture continues into three dimensions.

The second example has three unknowns:

2x − y = 0
−x + 2y − z = −1
−3y + 4z = 4.

Its matrix form is

[2−10−12−10−34][xyz]=[0−14]

A single linear equation in x, y, z describes a plane. For example, the second row is satisfied by (1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), and (0, −½, 0). These are the three points Strang uses to picture that plane.

The first row also describes a plane: it constrains x and y but leaves z free. The two planes intersect in a line. The third row contributes a third plane, and in this example the three planes meet at one point.

That common point is the solution of the system. The drawing indicates it by P; the next section identifies its coordinates. Strang’s point is that the row picture remains valid, but three intersecting planes are harder to read than two intersecting lines.

SECTION 0521:59–26:09

The third column is already the answer

Choose the combination before doing any elimination.

Read the same 3 × 3 system by columns:

x[2−10]+y[−12−3]+z[0−14]=[0−14]

The right-hand side b is identical to column 3. To produce it, take none of column 1, none of column 2, and one of column 3:

x = 0,   y = 0,   z = 1.

So P, the common point of the three planes, is (0, 0, 1). Substitution confirms it: the three left-hand sides become 0, −1, and 4, respectively.

This right-hand side was deliberately chosen to make the column picture easy. Strang notes that a systematic procedure is still needed for general systems; the following lecture introduces elimination.

SECTION 0626:09–27:48

Keep the columns; change the right-hand side

A second solution for the same coefficient matrix.

Keep A fixed but replace b by the sum of the first two columns:

[2−10]+[−12−3]=[11−3]

The required combination is now one of column 1, one of column 2, and none of column 3. Therefore the new solution is

x = 1,   y = 1,   z = 0.

Check the rows: 2(1) − 1 = 1; −1 + 2(1) − 0 = 1; and −3(1) + 4(0) = −3.

In the row picture, changing the right-hand sides changes the planes and their common point. In the column picture, the three column vectors stay fixed. Only the target b and the coefficients used to reach it change.

SECTION 0727:48–32:25

Can the columns reach every b?

The difference between a good square matrix and a singular one.

Solving one system leads to a more general question: can Ax = b be solved for every right-hand side b?

In three dimensions, the equivalent geometric question is whether the combinations of the three columns fill all of three-dimensional space. Strang says the answer is yes for the matrix in the worked example. He calls such a square matrix non-singular or invertible.

What can go wrong?

Suppose instead that all three columns lie in the same plane through the origin. For example, suppose column 3 is the sum of columns 1 and 2. Multiplying these columns by numbers and adding them never takes us outside that plane.

A right-hand side in the plane can be reached. A right-hand side outside it cannot. Thus the system is solvable for some b, but not for every b. That is the singular, non-invertible case described in the lecture.

The geometric test

To solve Ax = b for every b in three dimensions, the column combinations must fill the whole three-dimensional space.

SECTION 0832:25–35:33

The same question in nine dimensions

The picture becomes hard to draw; the algebraic idea stays the same.

Imagine nine equations in nine unknowns. A now has nine columns, and each column is a vector with nine components. We are still choosing a linear combination of the columns to reach a prescribed b.

9 × 9
Nine columns in ℝ⁹

Can their combinations reach every nine-component vector b?

The question does not depend on our ability to draw nine-dimensional space. If the columns supply enough independent directions, their combinations fill the whole space.

But suppose the ninth column simply repeats the eighth. It contributes no new direction. There are then right-hand sides that cannot be reached, just as a plane in three-dimensional space misses points outside it.

A precision note. Strang describes an “eight dimensional plane” as the typical outcome in this example. With a repeated column, the combinations occupy at most eight dimensions; they occupy exactly eight if the remaining eight columns are independent. This clarification is editorial.

SECTION 0935:33–39:29

Multiplication means combining columns

Two calculations, one result.

The lecture ends by making the column interpretation of Ax explicit. Strang uses a new matrix and a new vector:

[2513][12]=[127]

Compute a column at a time

The vector (1, 2)T asks for one copy of the first column and two copies of the second:

1[21]+2[53]=[127]

Compute a row at a time

The first row gives 2·1 + 5·2 = 12. The second gives 1·1 + 3·2 = 7. Strang identifies these row calculations with the dot products studied later in the course.

Both methods agree. The column method also explains the geometry of the system: the entries of the unknown vector tell us how much of each column to take.

“A times x is a combination of the columns of A.”

Gilbert Strang · Lecture 1, 38:24

If b were (12, 7)T for this new matrix, (1, 2)T would be the solution of Ax = b. The next lecture takes up the systematic method for finding solutions: elimination.
